[MUQATIL:83:1-5/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | A report about the pre-Islamic market says buyers received extra measure while sellers gave short measure, using two measures and two scales and shifting between them.
[FARRA:v3p245#2/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | اكتالوا على الناس means “took from people”; على and من alternate because the amount is owed to them, though the prepositions emphasize different sides of the transaction.
[MAJAZ:v1p14/r6] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Here على means ‘from’: they take full measure from the people.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p219/r6] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | The phrase إذا اكتالوا على الناس is glossed “from the people,” illustrating على in place of من.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p219/r7] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · صخر الغي | reports | Ṣakhr al-Ghayy’s على أقطارها is glossed من أقطارها, an example of على meaning من.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p300#3/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | In إذا اكتالوا على الناس يستوفون, على is glossed مع الناس (“with the people”).
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p300#3/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · صخر الغي | reports | The poet’s على أقطارها is glossed من أقطارها, showing على used with the sense من.
[TAB-FULL:v24p185#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī describes wayl as a valley of Hell’s pus for those who shortchange people in measures and weights, withholding their due full amount; mutaffif comes from something slight or scant.
[TAB-FULL:v24p185#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The expression people are equal like the taff of a measure means they are nearly level with a container that is almost, but not quite, full.
[TAB-FULL:v24p185#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله | reports | When told Medina’s people fulfill measures, ʿAbd Allāh answers that they should, since God warned the fraudulent through the verse about standing before the Lord. | mentions 83:1, 83:6
[TAB-FULL:v24p185#2/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عكرمة | reports | ʿIkrima swears that every measurer and weigher is in the Fire: none gives the same measure or weight that they themselves demand. | mentions 83:1
[TAB-FULL:v24p186/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī takes ʿalā and min as interchangeable when people take their full due, and parses hum in the next clause as the object pronoun for those being shortchanged.
[ZAJJAJ:v5p297/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | When they measure from others, they demand the full measure; likewise, when they buy by weight, they demand full weight.
[ZAJJAJ:v5p297/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The verse does not separately mention their weighing when buying because buying and selling involve goods measured or weighed.
[NAHHAS:v5p173/r6] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | reports | الذين may be a genitive adjective to المطففين or accusative as a condemnation; the latter better suits the verse.
[NAHHAS:v5p173/r7] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | اكتال عليه means taking what is owed from him, while اكتال منه means receiving the full measure from him; the expressions are not synonymous.
[THALABI:v10p149#3/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | When buyers take measure from people, على and من are interchangeable in this context.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p225#2/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | On acquiring measure from people, على means من; the cheater takes more than he is owed.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p309#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Iktiyāl means taking by measure, just as ittizān is taking by weight.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p309#2/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ says the phrase means they take from people; ʿalā and min alternate here because the buyer takes what is owed to him.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p309#2/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq says they demand full measure from people; the mention of measuring suffices for both measuring and weighing because either can stand for buying and selling.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p309#2/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · المفسرون | reports | The commentators mean that such people take full measure and weight when buying for themselves but reduce it when selling or weighing for others.
[JISHUMI:v10p7317/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Related usage describes an underfilled vessel and says all descendants of Adam are close to a full measure.
[JISHUMI:v10p7317/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | No one has superiority over another except through piety.
[JISHUMI:v10p7317/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · عامة القراء | reports | The common reading joins “they measure for them” as a transitive construction, with “them” as the object; ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar instead pauses after “they measure” and starts “they are defrauders” with “they” as subject, a reading attributed to Ḥamzah.
[JISHUMI:v10p7317/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | prefers | The author prefers the joined reading because the written form lacks an alif, Arabic says “I measured your due” meaning “for you,” and the readers unanimously use it.
[JISHUMI:v10p7317/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Ṭafīf means tiny or insignificant; a mutaffif reduces another person's proper measure or weight, whether by a small shortfall or a subtle theft.
[JISHUMI:v10p7317/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | One explanation names the act for the tiny amount missing from the rightful measure.
[JISHUMI:v10p7317/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Another view calls the act a secret theft of a small amount.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p362/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The wording means when they take a measure from people; min and ʿala can alternate in this construction.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p362/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says that when they buy for themselves, they take full measure and weight from others.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p719/r11] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Using ala where min might be expected signals that their taking from people harms and oppresses them.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p719/r12] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | Alternatively, ala attaches to yastawfun, with the object fronted to stress that they take full measure from others in particular while taking their own in full.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p719/r13] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra says min and ala alternate here: iktaltu alayka means I took what was due from you, while iktaltu minka means I received it from you.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p449#2/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الفراء والأخفش | reports | اكتالوا على الناس means taking measure from customers, while كالوهم means measuring for them; dropping the preposition makes the verb take an object.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p449#2/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو زيد | reports | Abu Zayd's verse illustrates the construction with an omitted prepositional complement.
[TABRISI:83:1-3/r16] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | When measuring what people owe them, they take the full amount; measuring is named while weighing is implied as its counterpart in trade.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p52/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · المفسرون واللغويون | reports | Interpreters and linguists take “ʿalā al-nās” as “from the people,” with ʿalā functioning like min.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p52/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ explains that “measuring against you” can mean taking the amount owed from you, while “measuring from you” means receiving full measure from you.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p52/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj says buyers who measure or weigh from others take the full amount; weighing is left implicit because goods are bought and sold by either measure or weight, and one indicates the other.
[RAZI-FULL:v31p80#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The preposition ʿalā in “they take from people” may signal harm and pressure imposed on them.
[RAZI-FULL:v31p80#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ says min and ʿalā alternate here because the amount is owed: taking from someone is taking what is due against him.
[QURTUBI-FULL:83:1-3/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس | reports | A Prophetic warning pairs five wrongs with consequences: broken covenants bring enemies, rejecting God's law poverty, immorality plague, short measure drought, and withholding alms the loss of rain.
[QURTUBI-FULL:83:1-3/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Al-Bazzar transmits the warning by gist, and Malik also relates it from Ibn ʿUmar.
[QURTUBI-FULL:83:1-3/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك بن دينار | reports | Malik ibn Dinar tells of a dying neighbor who used two measures and saw them grow into mountains of fire when struck together.
[QURTUBI-FULL:83:1-3/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عكرمة | reports | ʿIkrimah swears every measurer or weigher is destined for Hell, even when asked whether this applies to his son.
[QURTUBI-FULL:83:1-3/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Asmaʿi quotes a Bedouin saying manliness cannot reside in measure rims or scale tongues; it is also related from ʿAli.
[QURTUBI-FULL:83:1-3/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عبد خير | reports | ʿAbd Khayr says ʿAli overturned a scale that gave excess saffron, ordering accurate weight first and voluntary excess afterward.
[QURTUBI-FULL:83:1-3/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · نافع | reports | Nafiʿ says Ibn ʿUmar warned short-measurers will stand in sweat up to half their ears.
[QURTUBI-FULL:83:1-3/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abu Hurayrah says Medina's deputy recited this surah at dawn; he prayed against a trader who bought with full measure but sold short.
[QURTUBI-FULL:83:2-3/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra says ʿalā means “from”: buyers measuring from people insist on full measure.
[QURTUBI-FULL:83:2-3/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says they take extra for themselves but shortchange others, refusing people what they would refuse themselves.
[QURTUBI-FULL:83:2-3/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الطبري | reports | Al-Tabari glosses ʿalā as “at” or “with.”

3:1-2/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Cheaters take their dues from people in full; ʿalā instead of min marks a due owed by others or oppressive measuring against them.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p322#12/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | They demand complete measure when taking from people; على instead of من indicates that taking from people burdens and disadvantages them.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p322#12/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | The phrase may attach على to يستوفون, putting the object first to restrict their full measure to other people; al-Farrāʾ says من and على alternate here because the debt is owed.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p322#12/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ treats من and على as interchangeable here: taking from a person means collecting what is owed by that person.
[QASHANI:83:1-5/r1] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Beyond literal cheating in measures, the verses concern cheating on the true scale of justice, where character and deeds are measured.
[QASHANI:83:1-5/r2] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Such people overstate their own intellectual and practical virtues in relation to others from vanity and pride.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p424/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Taffif is reduction, from something tiny and insignificant; a mutaffif cheats by an inconspicuous small amount in weight or measure.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p425/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | When they measure for others, they collect what is due to themselves; when they measure or weigh for others, they make the recipients take less.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p426/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الفراء | reports | He says من and على alternate: measuring from someone means collecting one's due from them, while measuring on them means taking what they owe; Abu Hayyan prefers على as the direct complement of اكتالوا.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p426/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | He says على signals burdensome, harmful measuring, or it may attach to يستوفون to emphasize they take full measure from others while doing so for themselves.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p426/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | He says the apparent parsing attaches على to اكتالوا.
[SAMIN-DURR:83:2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The phrase على الناس can attach to اكتالوا; على and من alternate in this usage, and al-Farrāʾ distinguishes taking full measure from taking what is owed. The author calls this first analysis clearer.
[SAMIN-DURR:83:2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ says اكتلت على الناس means taking full measure from them, while اكتلت منهم means taking what they owe.
[SAMIN-DURR:83:2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Another analysis takes على as equivalent to من, as in the interchangeable expressions اكتلت عليه and اكتلت منه.
[SAMIN-DURR:83:2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī explains على in place of من as signaling that their taking full measure burdens and harms other people.
[SAMIN-DURR:83:2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | prefers | Al-Zamakhsharī also attaches على الناس to يستوفون: fronting it restricts their full measure to other people, while they secure it for themselves; al-Samīn calls this good.
[BURHAN:v3p165/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The author rejects the preceding analysis of كالوهم and وزنوهم on two grounds: the spelling lacks the alif expected by that reading, and الناس shows that the pronoun refers to the people; thus they take full measure from people but give people short measure.
[BURHAN:v3p342/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari says the verb carries the sense of تحاملوا, so it takes على although its usual complement is introduced by من.
[BURHAN:v3p342/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Transitivity usually follows the implied, omitted meaning rather than the expressed word; examples take الرفث as الإفضاء and drinking by a spring as being quenched by it. | mentions 4:187, 76:6
[BURHAN:v3p342/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي أبو بكر | reports | Al-Qadi Abu Bakr gives another definition of تضمين: a meaning conveyed without naming it, arising either from a word's form or from a phrase's semantic requirements.
[BURHAN:v3p342/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي أبو بكر | reports | One kind of implication follows from morphology: معلوم necessarily implies an عالم.
[BURHAN:v3p342/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي أبو بكر | reports | A second kind follows from the meaning of an expression, which cannot be realized without the implied complement: ضارب entails مضروب.
[BURHAN:v3p342/r8] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي أبو بكر | reports | Al-Qadi Abu Bakr calls all تضمين concise expression and treats the basmala as teaching people to begin acts in God's name for reverence or blessing.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p354#2/r10] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The verse omits ‘weigh’ when describing their own purchases because weighing offers less opportunity for deliberate extra fullness than measuring; shortchanging, however, is possible in both.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p354#2/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The preposition ʿalā portrays the fraudsters as acting from a position of superiority over customers; they demand full or more than full measure for themselves.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p354#2/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The expression may signal that they exploit anyone, especially a weak person; iktāl can take either min or ʿalā, while yastawfūn means they obtain complete measure eagerly and emphatically.
[BURSEVI:v10p282#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The relative clause explains how the cheaters shortchange others and why they merit condemnation: when receiving measured goods in a purchase, they take the full amount and more.
[BURSEVI:v10p282#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Iktiāl means taking goods by measure, like ittizān means taking by weight; ‘upon the people’ can imply dominance or seizure, not merely receiving one’s due.
[BURSEVI:v10p282#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Their istīfā’ is not fair receipt of an exact right but taking an abundant amount through any available trick, including packing measures, shaking them, and stealing from their rims and scale tongues.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p68#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The clause can define which defrauders are meant or describe their characteristic conduct: when taking from people in a sale, they demand a full, generous measure.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p68#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | One account says “against people” reflects the grasping force of taking over; another says it marks harm to people, since they obtain full measure by compaction, shaking, and similar tricks.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p68#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farraʾ says min and ʿala interchange here: they take in full what is owed to them by others.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p68#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Alusi reports objections: this gloss misses ordinary purchases from people to whom no debt is owed, and “taking in full” ordinarily means receiving one's due, so it alone does not explain the condemnation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p68#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Alusi answers that the paired conduct condemns them as in saying someone takes his due fully but gives others theirs short; this combination is blameworthy even if full receipt alone is proper.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p68#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Since a person's purchase from another usually concerns a due acquired through trade, al-Farraʾ may be describing the common case; the author invites consideration.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p68#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A proposed focus reading takes “against people” with “they take in full,” meaning they do so only against others, not themselves; critics say taking fully from oneself is not a plausible contrast.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p68#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Its defenders paraphrase the focus as harming others but not themselves, since they take extra from buyers while taking less when selling; Alusi remains unconvinced.
[ELMALILI:83:2-3/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The wording says buyers take full measure for themselves against people; using 'against' rather than 'from' signals acting to people's detriment, asserting power and insisting on full value.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p191/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Iktālū ʿalā al-nās means they bought measured goods from people; the measured object is omitted because the verb makes it understood.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p191/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The buyers' side mentions measuring alone because they usually bought produce by measure and paid in weighed coin; sellers use both measure and weight, revealing that the cheating was merchants' practice.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p192/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Yastawfūn answers “when”: istīfāʾ means taking the full amount, with the added letters intensifying the action.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p192/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The passage warns Muslims against widespread short-measure practices in early Medina and condemns the polytheists of Medina and Mecca.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p192/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Short measure combines injustice, theft, and meanness, traits the Arabs disdained separately yet practiced together.
[TABATABAI:83:1-5/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The sura opens by warning those who cheat in measure and weight that they will be resurrected for judgment on the Great Day, then describes the fates of wicked and righteous; context suggests the opening was revealed in Medina.
[TABATABAI:83:1-5/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Iktiyal means taking measured goods from people, with على signaling harm; Hijazi usage says kaalahu or wazanahu, which is the Qur'anic form, while other Arabs use kaala lahu or wazana lahu.

<<83:2 notes, part 2 of 0..2>>
 1402 · author | holds | They take their full due when buying but reduce what they give when selling, thereby making others lose.
[TABATABAI:83:1-5/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Both verses condemn one wrong: they insist on rights for themselves but deny others equal reciprocal rights, corrupting a society built on balanced claims.
[TABATABAI:83:1-5/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | rejects | One explanation says only buying by measure is mentioned because dealers commonly bought bulk grain and resold small amounts, usually by measure; the author finds this weak.
[TABATABAI:83:1-5/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | rejects | Another says weighing need not be mentioned when buying because weight and measure jointly indicate buying and selling; the author says the reasoning also applies to measures and is arbitrary.
[TABATABAI:83:1-5/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | rejects | A third explanation says the original cheats bought only by measure but sold by measure and weight; the author calls this an unsupported claim, and finds the other explanations weak too.
[ASAD-NOTES:83:1#n1/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · Asad | holds | The warning extends beyond commerce to every practical and moral social relation, including each person's rights, obligations, and possessions.
[ASAD-NOTES:83:1/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · Asad | holds | The condemned demand full measure when receiving from others but give less than their due when measuring or weighing what they owe.
[ASAD-NOTES:83:intro/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · Asad | reports | Authentic traditions cited by Tabari, Baghawi, and Ibn Kathir place at least the first four verses shortly after the Prophet's arrival in Medina.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p223/r1] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Sūrah al-Muṭaffifīn supplements al-Infiṭār, sharing its theme and elaborating the division of righteous and defiant people at its end.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p223/r2] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Al-Infiṭār reasons from God’s attributes displayed in the human body, while this sūrah reasons from the moral nature God gave people.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p223/r3] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Human nature loves justice and good and dislikes injustice and evil; this moral distinction shows that the Creator differentiates the just from the unjust rather than treating them alike.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p223/r4] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | People commit injustice when other motives overpower their nature, as shown by the dishonest trader who protests when others cheat him.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p223/r6] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The Qur’an repeatedly uses this reasoning for the Day of Judgement; the author points to his discussion of 75:14–15. | mentions 75:14, 75:15
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p224/r1] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Verses 1–6 censure people who demand fair treatment while cheating others; their conduct shows they do not expect to be raised before their Lord for judgement.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p226/r2] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Taṭfīf means giving short measure or weight.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p226/r3] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The verse contrasts people who insist on full measure from others with their own dishonesty toward others, exposing a moral inconsistency rather than merely naming a trading practice.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p227/r1] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Such a cheater knows justice requires the same honesty for both sides; he violates his own nature from selfishness, committing open and mean injustice.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p227/r2] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | God placed in people a moral barometer that makes them dislike oppression and like justice; when they oppress, desire or emotion overwhelms their ability to keep balance, not their ability to recognize right and wrong.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p227/r3] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Thieves, murderers, and adulterers would not want the same harm done to their own households, and even impartially acknowledge that society should protect life, wealth, and integrity for everyone.
